messages.content: You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

Please solve this issue: You are working on Campfire, a Rails chat application. Rooms, messages, memberships, and web push notifications are already in place; you will be extending them.

Feel free to store any design notes/insights that could be useful for future steps in the docs/ folder.

Follow the codebase conventions.

Our QA auto-tests drive the app in a browser and rely on the labels in quotes in each task. Keep them exactly as written, as visible text, a <label>, a placeholder, or an aria-label.

The QA auto-tests also expect:

- Switches are checkboxes (a styled switch is fine if a real checkbox sits under it).
- Confirmations use the browser's native `confirm()` dialog.

Let's add a new feature—bots. Bots can be members of rooms and post messages via an HTTP API.

Any chat member can create and manage bots via the user interface:
- open the account settings page (`/account/edit`)
- click the bot icon ("Set up chat bots")

This opens the bots page (`/bots`). It lists the bots you created (administrators see all bots) and has the "Add a chat bot" button. The button opens the `/bots/new` page with a form:

- bot avatar (optional)
- bot name (required), labelled "Name the bot"
- the "Save changes" button

Submitting the form creates a bot and redirects back to `/bots`. Each bot on the list shows its name and its unique bot code in a read-only field labelled "Bot code", in the same list item—the code is used to authenticate bot requests. The bot code is a sensitive credential. The bots page shows all of your bots on one page, without pagination.

From the list, you can also edit a bot (name, avatar): each bot has an "Edit <bot name>" link (for example, "Edit Deploy Bot") to its edit page. The edit page uses the same form and has a "Delete this chat bot" button that asks for confirmation. A deleted bot can no longer post messages.

Like any new user, a new bot joins all open rooms. Bots can be added to other rooms the same way as people.

Here is how a bot can post a message:

```
curl -d "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅" \
  https://chat.example.com/rooms/<room-id>/<bot-code>/messages
```

Bots can post from shell scripts and CI jobs. The raw request body becomes the message body. No JSON envelope, no field names.

The endpoint responds with:

- `201 Created` with `Location: /messages/:message_id`
- `422 Unprocessable Content` — empty body and no attachment
- `404 Not Found` — bad room id
- `401 Unauthorized` — invalid bot code

The message is broadcast to connected clients and triggers push notifications exactly as a human-authored message would.

The message shows the bot (its name) as the author.

      resources :transfers, only: %i[ show update ]
    end

      resources :users

      resource :join_code, only: :create
      resource :logo, only: %i[ show destroy ]
      resource :custom_styles, only: %i[ edit update ]
    end
  end

    route_for :account_logo, v: Current.account&.updated_at&.to_fs(:number), size: options[:size]
  end

  get "join/:join_code", to: "users#new", as: :join
  post "join/:join_code", to: "users#create"

  resources :qr_code, only: :show

  resources :users, only: :show do
    scope module: "users" do
      resource :avatar, only: %i[ show destroy ]
      resource :ban, only: %i[ create destroy ]

      scope defaults: { user_id: "me" } do
        resource :sidebar, only: :show
        resource :profile

          scope module: "push_subscriptions" do
            resources :test_notifications, only: :create
          end
        end
      end
    end
  end

  namespace :autocompletable do
    resources :users, only: :index
  end

    route_for :user_avatar, user.avatar_token, v: user.updated_at.to_fs(:number)
  end

    resources :messages

    scope module: "rooms" do
      resource :refresh, only: :show
      resource :settings, only: :show
      resource :involvement, only: %i[ show update ]
    end

  end

  get "service-worker" => "pwa#service_worker"

## Development

### Setting up

First, get everything installed and configured with:

```sh
bin/setup
```

This installs the system packages Campfire needs (SQLite, ffmpeg), the right Ruby version (via [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev)), and the app's gems; prepares the database; and starts Redis (in a Docker container called `campfire-redis`, if it isn't already running locally).

If you want to start over at any point, run:

```sh
bin/setup --reset
```

### Running the server

Start the development server with:

```sh
bin/dev
```

You'll be able to access the app at http://localhost:3000.

On first run you'll be guided through creating your admin account, and you can sign in with that account from then on.

Note that Campfire needs Redis (for Action Cable, caching, and background jobs), so if you've restarted your machine or stopped the container, `docker start campfire-redis` will bring it back.

### Web Push notifications

Campfire uses VAPID (Voluntary Application Server Identification) keys to send browser push notifications. For notifications to work in development you'll need to generate a key pair and set these environment variables:

- `VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY`
- `VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY`

You can generate a fresh pair (along with a secret key base, which you can ignore in development) by running:

```sh
script/admin/generate-secrets
```

### Running tests

Run the unit tests with:

```sh
bin/rails test
```

And the browser-based system tests with:

```sh
bin/rails test:system
```

Before pushing your changes, you can run the full CI suite locally - style checks, security audits, and all the tests - with a single command:

```sh
bin/ci
```

### Contributing

You are welcome - and encouraged - to modify Campfire to your liking.
If you'd like to contribute your changes back, please read our [contributing guide](../CONTRIBUTING.md) first.

## Development

### Setting up

First, get everything installed and configured with:

```sh
bin/setup
```

This installs the system packages Campfire needs (SQLite, ffmpeg), the right Ruby version (via [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev)), and the app's gems; prepares the database; and starts Redis (in a Docker container called `campfire-redis`, if it isn't already running locally).

If you want to start over at any point, run:

```sh
bin/setup --reset
```

### Running the server

Start the development server with:

```sh
bin/dev
```

You'll be able to access the app at http://localhost:3000.

On first run you'll be guided through creating your admin account, and you can sign in with that account from then on.

Note that Campfire needs Redis (for Action Cable, caching, and background jobs), so if you've restarted your machine or stopped the container, `docker start campfire-redis` will bring it back.

### Web Push notifications

Campfire uses VAPID (Voluntary Application Server Identification) keys to send browser push notifications. For notifications to work in development you'll need to generate a key pair and set these environment variables:

- `VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY`
- `VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY`

You can generate a fresh pair (along with a secret key base, which you can ignore in development) by running:

```sh
script/admin/generate-secrets
```

### Running tests

Run the unit tests with:

```sh
bin/rails test
```

And the browser-based system tests with:

```sh
bin/rails test:system
```

Before pushing your changes, you can run the full CI suite locally - style checks, security audits, and all the tests - with a single command:

```sh
bin/ci
```

### Contributing

You are welcome - and encouraged - to modify Campfire to your liking.
If you'd like to contribute your changes back, please read our [contributing guide](../CONTRIBUTING.md) first.

class Room < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :memberships, dependent: :delete_all do
    def grant_to(users)
      room = proxy_association.owner
      Membership.insert_all(Array(users).collect { |user| { room_id: room.id, user_id: user.id, involvement: room.default_involvement } })
    end

    def revoke_from(users)
      destroy_by user: users
    end

    def revise(granted: [], revoked: [])
      transaction do
        grant_to(granted) if granted.present?
        revoke_from(revoked) if revoked.present?
      end
    end
  end

  has_many :users, through: :memberships
  has_many :messages, dependent: :destroy

  belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", default: -> { Current.user }

  validate :direct_rooms_keep_their_type, on: :update

  scope :opens,           -> { where(type: "Rooms::Open") }
  scope :closeds,         -> { where(type: "Rooms::Closed") }
  scope :directs,         -> { where(type: "Rooms::Direct") }
  scope :without_directs, -> { where.not(type: "Rooms::Direct") }

  scope :ordered, -> { order("LOWER(name)") }

  class << self
    def create_for(attributes, users:)
      transaction do
        create!(attributes).tap do |room|
          room.memberships.grant_to users
        end
      end
    end

    def original
      order(:created_at).first
    end
  end

  def receive(message)
    unread_memberships(message)
    push_later(message)
  end

  def open?
    is_a?(Rooms::Open)
  end

  def closed?
    is_a?(Rooms::Closed)
  end

  def direct?
    is_a?(Rooms::Direct)
  end

  def default_involvement
    "mentions"
  end

  private
    # Open and closed rooms convert into each other freely. A direct room can't become
    # either: its participants agreed to a private conversation, not to one whose
    # audience someone else gets to widen afterwards.
    def direct_rooms_keep_their_type
      if type_changed? && type_was == "Rooms::Direct"
        errors.add :type, "can't be changed for a direct room"
      end
    end

    def unread_memberships(message)
      memberships.visible.disconnected.where.not(user: message.creator).update_all(unread_at: message.created_at, updated_at: Time.current)
    end

    def push_later(message)
      Room::PushMessageJob.perform_later(self, message)
    end
end

  attr_reader :room, :message

  def initialize(room:, message:)
    @room, @message = room, message
  end

  def push
    build_payload.tap do |payload|
      push_to_users_involved_in_everything(payload)
      push_to_users_involved_in_mentions(payload)
    end
  end

  private
    def build_payload
      if room.direct?
        build_direct_payload
      else
        build_shared_payload
      end
    end

    def build_direct_payload
      {
        title: message.creator.name,
        body: message.plain_text_body,
        path: Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.room_path(room)
      }
    end

    def build_shared_payload
      {
        title: room.name,
        body: "#{message.creator.name}: #{message.plain_text_body}",
        path: Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.room_path(room)
      }
    end

    def push_to_users_involved_in_everything(payload)
      enqueue_payload_for_delivery payload, push_subscriptions_for_users_involved_in_everything
    end

    def push_to_users_involved_in_mentions(payload)
      enqueue_payload_for_delivery payload, push_subscriptions_for_mentionable_users(message.mentionees)
    end

    def push_subscriptions_for_users_involved_in_everything
      relevant_subscriptions.merge(Membership.involved_in_everything)

  attr_reader :room, :message

  def initialize(room:, message:)
    @room, @message = room, message
  end

  def push
    build_payload.tap do |payload|
      push_to_users_involved_in_everything(payload)
      push_to_users_involved_in_mentions(payload)
    end
  end

  private
    def build_payload
      if room.direct?
        build_direct_payload
      else
        build_shared_payload
      end
    end

    def build_direct_payload
      {
        title: message.creator.name,
        body: message.plain_text_body,
        path: Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.room_path(room)
      }
    end

    def build_shared_payload
      {
        title: room.name,
        body: "#{message.creator.name}: #{message.plain_text_body}",
        path: Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.room_path(room)
      }
    end

    def push_to_users_involved_in_everything(payload)
      enqueue_payload_for_delivery payload, push_subscriptions_for_users_involved_in_everything
    end

    def push_to_users_involved_in_mentions(payload)

      Push::Subscription
        .joins(user: :memberships)
        .merge(Membership.visible.disconnected.where(room: room).where.not(user: message.creator))
    end

module Authentication
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern
  include SessionLookup

  included do
    before_action :require_authentication
    helper_method :signed_in?

    protect_from_forgery with: :exception
  end

  class_methods do
    def allow_unauthenticated_access(**options)
      skip_before_action :require_authentication, **options
    end

    def require_unauthenticated_access(**options)
      skip_before_action :require_authentication, **options
      before_action :restore_authentication, :redirect_signed_in_user_to_root, **options
    end
  end

  private
    def signed_in?
      Current.user.present?
    end

    def require_authentication
      restore_authentication || request_authentication
    end

    def restore_authentication
      if session = find_session_by_cookie
        resume_session session
      end
    end

    def request_authentication
      session[:return_to_after_authenticating] = request.url
      redirect_to new_session_url
    end

    def redirect_signed_in_user_to_root
      redirect_to root_url if signed_in?
    end

    def start_new_session_for(user)
      user.sessions.start!(user_agent: request.user_agent, ip_address: request.remote_ip).tap do |session|
        authenticated_as session
      end
    end

    def resume_session(session)
      session.resume user_agent: request.user_agent, ip_address: request.remote_ip
      authenticated_as session
    end

    def terminate_current_session
      Current.session&.destroy!
      reset_session
      remove_authentication_cookie
    end

    def authenticated_as(session)
      Current.session = session
      set_authentication_cookie(session)
    end

    def post_authenticating_url
      session.delete(:return_to_after_authenticating) || root_url
    end

    def set_authentication_cookie(session)
      cookies.signed.permanent[:session_token] = { value: session.token, httponly: true, same_site: :lax }
    end

    def remove_authentication_cookie
      cookies.delete(:session_token)
    end
end

module Authentication
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern
  include SessionLookup

  included do
    before_action :require_authentication
    helper_method :signed_in?

    protect_from_forgery with: :exception
  end

  class_methods do
    def allow_unauthenticated_access(**options)
      skip_before_action :require_authentication, **options
    end

    def require_unauthenticated_access(**options)
      skip_before_action :require_authentication, **options
      before_action :restore_authentication, :redirect_signed_in_user_to_root, **options
    end
  end

  private
    def signed_in?
      Current.user.present?
    end

    def require_authentication
      restore_authentication || request_authentication
    end

    def restore_authentication
      if session = find_session_by_cookie
        resume_session session
      end
    end

    def request_authentication
      session[:return_to_after_authenticating] = request.url
      redirect_to new_session_url
    end

    def redirect_signed_in_user_to_root
      redirect_to root_url if signed_in?
    end

    def start_new_session_for(user)
      user.sessions.start!(user_agent: request.user_agent, ip_address: request.remote_ip).tap do |session|
        authenticated_as session
      end
    end

    def resume_session(session)
      session.resume user_agent: request.user_agent, ip_address: request.remote_ip
      authenticated_as session
    end

    def terminate_current_session
      Current.session&.destroy!
      reset_session
      remove_authentication_cookie
    end

    def authenticated_as(session)
      Current.session = session
      set_authentication_cookie(session)
    end

    def post_authenticating_url
      session.delete(:return_to_after_authenticating) || root_url
    end

    def set_authentication_cookie(session)
      cookies.signed.permanent[:session_token] = { value: session.token, httponly: true, same_site: :lax }
    end

    def remove_authentication_cookie
      cookies.delete(:session_token)
    end
end

    @room  = Rooms::Closed.new(name: DEFAULT_ROOM_NAME)
    @users = User.active.ordered
  end

  def create
    room = Rooms::Closed.create_for(room_params, users: grantees)

    broadcast_create_room(room)
    redirect_to room_url(room)
  end

  def edit
    selected_user_ids = @room.users.pluck(:id)
    @selected_users, @unselected_users = User.active.ordered.partition { |user| selected_user_ids.include?(user.id) }
  end

  def update
    @room.update! room_params
    @room.memberships.revise(granted: grantees, revoked: revokees)

    broadcast_update_room
    redirect_to room_url(@room)

    # rooms never are: converting one would let its creator revise who's in it.
    def room_scope
      Current.user.rooms.without_directs
    end

    def grantees
      User.where(id: grantee_ids)
    end

    def revokees
      @room.users.where.not(id: grantee_ids)
    end

    def grantee_ids
      params.fetch(:user_ids, [])
    end

        broadcast_prepend_to user, :rooms, target: :shared_rooms, html: html
      end
    end

    def broadcast_update_room
      each_user_and_html_for(@room) do |user, html|
        broadcast_replace_to user, :rooms, target: [ @room, :list ], html: html
      end
    end

    def each_user_and_html_for(room)
      # Optimization to avoid rendering the same partial for every user
      html = render_to_string(partial: "users/sidebars/rooms/shared", locals: { room: room })

      room.users.each { |user| yield user, html }

class RoomsController < ApplicationController
  before_action :set_room, only: %i[ show destroy ]
  before_action :ensure_can_administer, only: %i[ destroy ]
  before_action :remember_last_room_visited, only: :show

  def index
    redirect_to room_url(Current.user.rooms.last)
  end

  def show
    @messages = find_messages
  end

  def destroy
    @room.destroy

    broadcast_remove_room
    redirect_to root_url
  end

  private
    def set_room
      if room = room_scope.find_by(id: params[:room_id] || params[:id])
        @room = room
      else
        redirect_to root_url, alert: "Room not found or inaccessible"
      end
    end

    # Subclasses narrow this to the room types they're allowed to act on, so that one
    # room namespace can't be used to reach another's rooms.
    def room_scope
      Current.user.rooms
    end

    def ensure_can_administer
      head :forbidden unless Current.user.can_administer?(@room)
    end

    def ensure_permission_to_create_rooms
      if Current.account.settings.restrict_room_creation_to_administrators? && !Current.user.administrator?
        head :forbidden
      end
    end

    def find_messages
      messages = @room.messages.with_creator.with_attachment_details.with_boosts

      if show_first_message = messages.find_by(id: params[:message_id])
        @messages = messages.page_around(show_first_message)
      else
        @messages = messages.last_page
      end
    end

    def room_params
      params.require(:room).permit(:name)
    end

    def broadcast_remove_room
      broadcast_remove_to :rooms, target: [ @room, :list ]
    end
end

class Rooms::ClosedsController < RoomsController
  before_action :set_room, only: %i[ show edit update ]
  before_action :ensure_can_administer, only: %i[ update ]
  before_action :remember_last_room_visited, only: :show
  before_action :force_room_type, only: %i[ edit update ]
  before_action :ensure_permission_to_create_rooms, only: %i[ new create ]

  DEFAULT_ROOM_NAME = "New room"

  def show
    redirect_to room_url(@room)
  end

  def new
    @room  = Rooms::Closed.new(name: DEFAULT_ROOM_NAME)
    @users = User.active.ordered
  end

  def create
    room = Rooms::Closed.create_for(room_params, users: grantees)

    broadcast_create_room(room)
    redirect_to room_url(room)
  end

  def edit
    selected_user_ids = @room.users.pluck(:id)
    @selected_users, @unselected_users = User.active.ordered.partition { |user| selected_user_ids.include?(user.id) }
  end

  def update
    @room.update! room_params
    @room.memberships.revise(granted: grantees, revoked: revokees)

    broadcast_update_room
    redirect_to room_url(@room)
  end

  private
    # Allows us to edit an open room and turn it into a closed one on saving.
    def force_room_type
      @room = @room.becomes!(Rooms::Closed)
    end

    # Open and closed rooms convert into each other, so both are in reach here. Direct
    # rooms never are: converting one would let its creator revise who's in it.
    def room_scope
      Current.user.rooms.without_directs
    end

    def grantees
      User.where(id: grantee_ids)
    end

    def revokees
      @room.users.where.not(id: grantee_ids)
    end

    def grantee_ids
      params.fetch(:user_ids, [])
    end

    def broadcast_create_room(room)
      each_user_and_html_for(room) do |user, html|
        broadcast_prepend_to user, :rooms, target: :shared_rooms, html: html
      end
    end

    def broadcast_update_room
      each_user_and_html_for(@room) do |user, html|
        broadcast_replace_to user, :rooms, target: [ @room, :list ], html: html
      end
    end

    def each_user_and_html_for(room)
      # Optimization to avoid rendering the same partial for every user
      html = render_to_string(partial: "users/sidebars/rooms/shared", locals: { room: room })

      room.users.each { |user| yield user, html }
    end
end

      Rails.application.executor.wrap do
        Rails.logger.info "Destroying push subscription: #{subscription_id}"
        Push::Subscription.find_by(id: subscription_id)&.destroy
      end
    end
  )

  at_exit { config.x.web_push_pool.shutdown }
end

module WebPush::PersistentRequest
  def perform
    if @options[:connection]
      http = @options[:connection]
    else
      http = Net::HTTP.new(uri.host, uri.port, *proxy_options)
      http.use_ssl = true
      http.ssl_timeout = @options[:ssl_timeout] unless @options[:ssl_timeout].nil?
      http.open_timeout = @options[:open_timeout] unless @options[:open_timeout].nil?
      http.read_timeout = @options[:read_timeout] unless @options[:read_timeout].nil?
    end

    req = Net::HTTP::Post.new(uri.request_uri, headers)
    req.body = body

    if http.is_a?(Net::HTTP::Persistent)
      response = http.request uri, req
    else
      resp = http.request(req)
      verify_response(resp)
    end

    resp
  end
end

module WebPush::PersistentRequest
  def perform
    if @options[:connection]
      http = @options[:connection]
    else
      http = Net::HTTP.new(uri.host, uri.port, *proxy_options)
      http.use_ssl = true
      http.ssl_timeout = @options[:ssl_timeout] unless @options[:ssl_timeout].nil?
      http.open_timeout = @options[:open_timeout] unless @options[:open_timeout].nil?
      http.read_timeout = @options[:read_timeout] unless @options[:read_timeout].nil?
    end

    req = Net::HTTP::Post.new(uri.request_uri, headers)
    req.body = body

    if http.is_a?(Net::HTTP::Persistent)
      response = http.request uri, req
    else
      resp = http.request(req)
      verify_response(resp)
    end

    resp
  end
end

require "application_system_test_case"

class SendingMessagesTest < ApplicationSystemTestCase
  setup do
    sign_in "jz@37signals.com"
    join_room rooms(:designers)
  end

  test "sending messages between two users" do
    using_session("Kevin") do
      sign_in "kevin@37signals.com"
      join_room rooms(:designers)
    end

    join_room rooms(:designers)
    send_message "Is this thing on?"

    using_session("Kevin") do
      join_room rooms(:designers)
      assert_message_text "Is this thing on?"

      send_message "👍👍"
    end

    join_room rooms(:designers)
    assert_message_text "👍👍"
  end

  test "editing messages" do
    using_session("Kevin") do
      sign_in "kevin@37signals.com"
      join_room rooms(:designers)
    end

    within_message messages(:third) do
      reveal_message_actions
      find(".message__edit-btn").click
      fill_in_rich_text_area "message_body", with: "Redacted!"
      click_on "Save changes"
    end

    using_session("Kevin") do
      join_room rooms(:designers)

      assert_message_text "Redacted!"
    end
  end

  test "deleting messages" do
    using_session("Kevin") do
      sign_in "kevin@37signals.com"
      join_room rooms(:designers)

      assert_message_text "Third time's a charm."
    end

    within_message messages(:third) do
      reveal_message_actions
      find(".message__edit-btn").click

      accept_confirm do
        click_on "Delete message"
      end
    end

    using_session("Kevin") do
      assert_message_text "Third time's a charm.", count: 0
    end
  end
end

**Architectural Deep Dive into User Management with Bots**

Okay, this is fascinating. This `grep` output gives us a crystal-clear view of how the `User` model is utilized in Campfire, and where we need to consider bots. My initial reaction is that we need to examine every usage with extreme care.

Based on the prompt, it seems bots are essentially "users" in the system, but with distinct behaviors and lifecycle management. They are *users* that can be created, edited, and deleted. So it appears that bots should simply be a special type of user (e.g., `role: :bot`) or have a concern like `User::Bot`.

Let's break down where `User` is used and consider the bot implications for each:

1.  **Messages**: The `Message` model has a `creator`, which *belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User"*. No special consideration here, a bot is just another message creator. But now we have to check how the creator is *rendered*. `avatar_tag` is the key thing, we need to ensure that the rendering of a bot user doesn't expose sensitive info. This is likely the single biggest thing to consider in all these "user" instances!
2.  **Memberships**: `Membership` *belongs_to :user* and tracks rooms. New bots should join open rooms automatically (as the prompt mentions), and can be added to other rooms "the same way as people," which means through the existing membership system.
3.  **User Model Itself**:
    *   `has_many :memberships`, `has_many :rooms, through: :memberships` - all good.
    *   `has_one_attached :avatar` – applies to bots as well, which is great, since we can let users upload bot avatars. This also needs careful inspection, to see if the user’s images could be used by bots, or if the bot is given its own images path.
    *   `after_create_commit :grant_membership_to_open_rooms` – Perfect. New bots get added to open rooms automatically.
    *   **Controllers** (`Rooms::ClosedsController`, `Rooms::OpensController`, etc.):
        *   These controllers control adding *users* to rooms. This is where the prompt's instruction to handle bots the same way as humans is most relevant. We need to confirm that bots are included in the user lists for room management:
            *   Open room management includes bots in the user list.
            *   Closed room management should include bots in the switches for adding/removing members.
            *   Direct rooms must allow starting a ping with a bot.
        *   `Autocompletable::UsersController` (used in direct rooms) – This must include bots in the autocomplete results.
    *   **`deactivate` method**: The existing `deactivate` method handles user deactivation. This is where things get interesting, because bots should probably not be “deactivated” in the same sense as human users. Deleting a bot means it can no longer post messages, so `deactivate` probably needs special handling for bot instances. We also need to be sure that the existing `delete_all` calls are safe for bot data!
4.  **`app/views/messages/_message.html.erb`**: This is key! This is where the *user* is rendered as the message author! We need to ensure the rendering of a bot’s avatar and name doesn’t expose anything sensitive (e.g., mail_to link, or a transfer button). If you click a bot’s avatar, it links to `user_path(bot_user)`.
5.  **`users` Table Schema**:
    *   `email_address` is nullable, which is good. We can have bots without email addresses.
    *   `password_digest` – bots likely won’t have passwords, unless we use them as "login" tokens, so we'll need to use `""` or `nil` instead of a password.
    *   If a bot has `email_address: nil`, the existing authentication code could be flawed, and need handling (`SessionsController#create`). If the bot doesn't have a password or an email, we need to modify the authentication and authorization flows and make sure this is handled correctly.
6.  **Account Management (`/account/edit`):**
    *   The prompt specifies separate management for bots, so bots should *not* appear in the list of account members.
    *   **Bots are managed at `/bots`**. We need to ensure that this is enforced everywhere. The `AccountsController` and `Accounts::UsersController` should *exclude* bots from the account user

**Analyzing Bot Integration in Campfire**

Okay, first things first, my mind is racing looking at this code. I need to make sure I understand how bots will integrate into the existing user flow, and if the current implementation holds up. I'm focusing on the `direct_placeholder` feature in the sidebar and how it handles new direct rooms. The key is in `app/views/users/sidebars/rooms/_direct_placeholder.html.erb` and the associated controller method, `Users::SidebarsController#find_direct_placeholder_users`. I'm seeing that this displays a "Start a ping with <FirstName>" button. This whole approach for direct rooms is crucial, especially when we're dealing with accounts with fewer than 20 users. We need to be able to add bots through the same routes. We can add to direct rooms with 'New Ping' or by clicking on the bot's avatar as well.

The existing code lets people add users to open and closed rooms via checkbox switches (`Give <name> access to this room`). Direct rooms use `Autocompletable::UsersController`, meaning the logic in that controller is used to autocomplete the names, and `Users::SidebarsController`, suggesting that the existing functionality is using `User.active.where.not(id: exclude_user_ids)`. But, I'm thinking, should bots be treated the same here? Should they be in `direct_placeholder_users`?

If bots are indeed just treated like any other active user in all rooms (`open`, `closed`, and `direct`), then a bot could be added to a direct room just by clicking "Start a ping with <bot>". That's a good thing!

I need to make sure this doesn't break anything. Checking `Autocompletable::UsersController`, it looks like it's used in two places: to autocomplete user selection in the "New Ping" form and for rich `@mention` autocompletion in the Trix composer. I see that the JSON generated for `@mentions` includes avatar URLs and SGIDs using the `fresh_user_avatar_url(user)` method, but does this work on a bot? Looking through the code, it looks like it does.

Will adding bots to `direct_placeholder_users` break any tests? I'm going to have to check if existing tests will be affected if we start including bots in fixtures. I need to check how fixtures are structured and how many tests check the existing user count. I need to look closely at `test/controllers/accounts_controller_test.rb`, `test/models/room/push_test.rb`, and other tests. I'm especially concerned about tests that might check `User.count` or other related counts.

Then, there's the question of deleting bots. The prompt mentions a "Delete this chat bot" button that calls the edit page for confirmation. What happens when a bot is deleted? The prompt says "A deleted bot can no longer post messages."

I need to consider soft deletes vs hard deletes (`bot.deactivate` vs `bot.destroy`). I see that `User` has `has_many :messages, dependent: :destroy, foreign_key: :creator_id`. Wait, wait, wait, if `bot.destroy` is called, all messages associated with the bot will be DESTROYED! That's bad. That's not how human users are deleted. Human users are `deactivate`d in `Accounts::UsersController#destroy`. `User#deactivate` is what the Campfire authors wanted - it keeps the bot's messages, just deactivates the bot.

`@user.deactivate` does several things: it deletes memberships for open and closed rooms, but *not* direct rooms (to preserve display names!), and it updates the status to `:deactivated` and updates the email. What about direct rooms? If a deleted bot is in a Direct room (Ping), and then someone tries to send a message via curl? `401 Unauthorized` is returned! When the bot is looked up, it won't be found because it's no longer considered active. When a deactivated bot's avatar is clicked, the app shows "<Bot Name> is no longer on this account"!

I'm noticing that the Campfire authors already used safe navigation (`email_address&.gsub`)! And the email address is nullable! This hints that the system was built for this from the start.

I need to look for any other subtle clues or coding conventions! Time to review more tests.

**Comprehensive Bot Code Security Review**

Okay, let's break down this `/bots` requirement like a pro.

Firstly, regarding authorization, it's immediately clear that we need granular control. When a bot is created, we'll store its creator's ID. Leveraging `User::Role#can_administer?` in `app/models/user/role.rb`, we can neatly define access. If a user is an administrator, they see everything, naturally. The creator of a bot also has full control. Everyone else? They only see their *own* bots. The system should scope the lookup for edit, update, and destroy actions too, giving a 403 or 404 if the current user lacks the necessary permission. The same conventions are used across the codebase, in `MessagesController`, and `RoomsController`.

Now, let's dissect the presentation of the bots on the `/bots` page. Each bot gets its own list item. Inside that item, we'll show its avatar and name, a read-only field labeled "Bot code" *and* an "Edit" link. And, given that the bot code is a "sensitive credential," we must consider everything this implies.

The core question is: why did the prompt call the bot code a "sensitive credential"? Is it about the fact that it is an API key?

It's clear that several security implications MUST be considered.
1.  **Logging**: We HAVE to filter that parameter in our logs. The Rails `filter_parameter_logging.rb` initializer is key here. Make sure `:bot_code` and `:bot_key` are in there, or use a more broad filter such as `:token` or `:_key`.
2.  **Generation**: The bot code must be a cryptographically random token. I'm thinking `SecureRandom.alphanumeric(12)`, or maybe the `has_secure_token :bot_token` helper. We need high entropy.
3.  **Authentication**: We need to use *constant-time* comparison. This is the classic timing-attack vulnerability! If the bot code is just a simple token that we store in the database, we'll use `ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare`. However, if we follow the pattern in Campfire (and it looks like a good one!), the bot code could be a combined key like "<bot\_id>-<bot\_token>". The bot token has to be generated in such a way that it never contains "-" so splitting on the hyphen ALWAYS returns an array of two, with the ID on the left and the token on the right. When we get the bot code via an API call, we can split it, look up the bot by the ID (easy), and then use `secure_compare` with the token. Also, it should be a key that does not require any URL encoding to send.
4.  **UI Considerations**: This "sensitive credential" thing is critical for the UI/UX. We will set the input type to "text" and the `readonly` attribute. The text inside WILL be shown. We *don't* want to use `<input type="password">` because even in this case, a QA test can read the value of the input. We are explicitly showing the bot code to the user.
5.  **Visibility**: The prompt explicitly notes that only the creator and admins can *see* the bot code. We MUST ensure that the bot code is never exposed in user profiles, autocomplete lists, or messages. The authorization logic has to be rock solid.
6.  **Deactivation**: When a bot is deleted, we invalidate the token or mark the bot as "deactivated", ensuring that the code is no longer usable.

Now, with the `<id>-<token>` pattern, we're guaranteed a globally unique, URL-safe bot key. The authentication uses a fast primary key lookup (which is fine), and the token comparison in constant time. And that, I believe, is rock-solid secure.

Okay, so I've been digging into this backtrace, and it's a real eye-opener.  We've got this chain of events:  `Rack::MethodOverride` -> `Rack::Request::Helpers#POST` -> `Rack::QueryParser#parse_query_pairs` -> `URI._decode_uri_component`. The problem arises when `curl` sends data, typically with `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`.  Even before our routing gets involved, `Rack::MethodOverride` in the Rack middleware tries to parse this as a form, looking for `_method` to override the HTTP method.  It rescues the `Rack::Utils::InvalidParameterError` but then `ActionController::Instrumentation#process_action` ends up calling `request.filtered_parameters` -> `request.parameters` -> `ActionDispatch::Request#POST`. The key here is that `POST` DOES NOT rescue that error, raising `ActionController::BadRequest (400)` instead!

Even worse, what if the `Content-Type` is set to `application/json` but the data is garbage?  `ActionDispatch::Http::Parameters` would then throw a `ParseError`!

We have a real problem because the prompt specifies that raw request bodies are expected from shell scripts and CI jobs, without any JSON envelope.

The fix?  It looks like we can cleanly address this at either the Rack middleware layer or the controller level in `process_action`.  Since `Rack::MethodOverride` already catches the error, we can intervene before it gets to the controller:

We can insert a tiny Rack middleware (or override `process_action` / `wrap_parameters false` + `request.set_header("CONTENT_TYPE", "text/plain")` for `/rooms/:room_id/:bot_key/messages` when not `multipart/form-data`! Wait: what if in a future step attachments are posted via `multipart/form-data` or raw binary? Notice if `CONTENT_TYPE` is `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `curl -d` sets `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` ONLY because `-d` defaults to that when posting a raw text body!).

I'm thinking, in `BotMessagesController`, we'd set `wrap_parameters false` and *before* `super` in `process_action`: We can nullify `request.request_parameters = {}`. #### **Location Header:**

The `Location: /messages/:message_id` header is key. It provides a relative path, `/messages/:message_id`, and not a full URL. My initial thought was `room_message_url`, but then I saw `message_path(@message)` already exists in `config/routes.rb`. `Message#to_param` is overridden, returning the numeric ID. So, `message_path(@message)` will return `"/messages/#{@message.id}"`.  This is important. Then, if Rails `head :created, location: "/messages/123"` keeps the path *relative*, that is *critical.* I need to verify that `response.headers["Location"]` will literally be `"/messages/#{@message.id}"` and not be expanded. I'll test this in `bin/rails runner` to be absolutely certain.

#### **Response Order:**

The order of error checking, `401 Unauthorized`, `404 Not Found`, and `422 Unprocessable Content`, needs to be precise.  Security must come first. Authentication must run before anything else to prevent unauthorized probes of room IDs. So, `401 Unauthorized` before `set_room`.

Now, if a bot code is valid, but the room ID is bad, it should return a `404 Not Found`.

**A major catch:** What if the room ID *exists* but is a closed or direct room and the bot isn't a member? This is handled with the `room_scoped.rb` concern. It looks like when `Current.user` is `@bot`, using `@bot.rooms.find(params[:room_id])` raises `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound` so we will get a `404 Not Found`. class ContentFilters::RemoveSoloUnfurledLinkText < ActionText::Content::Filter
  def applicable?
    normalize_tweet_url(solo_unfurled_url) == normalize_tweet_url(content.to_plain_text)
  end

  def apply
    fragment.replace("div") { |node| node.tap { |n| n.inner_html = unfurled_links.first.to_s } }
  end

  private
    TWITTER_DOMAINS = %w[ x.com twitter.com ]
    TWITTER_DOMAIN_MAPPING = { "x.com" => "twitter.com" }

    def solo_unfurled_url
      unfurled_links.first["href"] if unfurled_links.size == 1
    end

    def unfurled_links
      fragment.find_all("action-text-attachment[@content-type='#{ActionText::Attachment::OpengraphEmbed::OPENGRAPH_EMBED_CONTENT_TYPE}']")
    end

    def normalize_tweet_url(url)
      return url unless twitter_url?(url)

      uri = URI.parse(url)

      uri.dup.tap do |u|
        u.host = TWITTER_DOMAIN_MAPPING[uri.host&.downcase] || uri.host
        u.query = nil
      end.to_s
    rescue URI::InvalidURIError
      url
    end

    def twitter_url?(url)
      url.present? && TWITTER_DOMAINS.any? { |domain| url.strip.include?(domain) }
    end
end

class ContentFilters::SanitizeAttributes < ActionText::Content::Filter
  def applicable?
    true
  end

  # Scrub attributes on the tags that SanitizeTags allows, using Rails' safe-list
  # sanitizer so unsafe URI schemes and event-handler attributes are stripped.
  # Runs after SanitizeTags, so passing the same allowed tags makes the tag pass
  # a no-op and only attributes are scrubbed.
  def apply
    sanitizer.sanitize fragment.to_html, tags: allowed_tags, attributes: allowed_attributes
  end

  private
    # Presentation styling relies on class attributes (e.g. unfurled link embeds),
    # which the standard ActionText set doesn't include.
    EXTRA_ALLOWED_ATTRIBUTES = %w[ class ]

    # ActionText::ContentHelper.sanitizer is a single process-wide instance, and
    # rails-html-sanitizer reuses one mutable permit scrubber that it reconfigures
    # from the tags/attributes on every #sanitize call. Sharing it here would race
    # our stricter tag set against ActionText's default rendering on concurrent
    # requests, so use a dedicated instance of the same sanitizer class to keep the
    # scrubber isolated.
    def sanitizer
      sanitizer_class.new
    end

    def sanitizer_class
      ActionText::ContentHelper.sanitizer.class
    end

    def allowed_tags
      ContentFilters::SanitizeTags::ALLOWED_TAGS
    end

    def allowed_attributes
      standard_allowed_attributes + EXTRA_ALLOWED_ATTRIBUTES
    end

    # Mirrors ActionText::ContentHelper#sanitizer_allowed_attributes, which isn't
    # exposed at the module level.
    def standard_allowed_attributes
      ActionText::ContentHelper.allowed_attributes ||
        (sanitizer_class.allowed_attributes + ActionText::Attachment::ATTRIBUTES).to_a
    end
end

class ContentFilters::SanitizeTags < ActionText::Content::Filter
  def applicable?
    true
  end

  def apply
    fragment.replace(not_allowed_tags_css_selector) { nil }
  end

  private
    ALLOWED_TAGS = %w[ a abbr acronym address b big blockquote br cite code dd del dfn div dl dt em h1 h2 h3 h4 h5 h6 hr i ins kbd li ol
      p pre samp small span strong sub sup time tt ul var ] + [ ActionText::Attachment.tag_name, "figure", "figcaption" ]

    def not_allowed_tags_css_selector
      ALLOWED_TAGS.map { |tag| ":not(#{tag})" }.join("")
    end
end

class ContentFilters::StyleUnfurledTwitterAvatars < ActionText::Content::Filter
  def applicable?
    unfurled_twitter_avatars.present?
  end

  def apply
    fragment.update do |source|
      div = source.at_css("div")
      div["class"] = UNFURLED_TWITTER_AVATAR_CSS_CLASS
    end
  end

  private
    UNFURLED_TWITTER_AVATAR_CSS_CLASS = "cf-twitter-avatar"

    def unfurled_twitter_avatars
      fragment.find_all("#{opengraph_css_selector}[url*='#{TWITTER_AVATAR_URL_PREFIX}']")
    end

    def opengraph_css_selector
      "action-text-attachment[@content-type='#{ActionText::Attachment::OpengraphEmbed::OPENGRAPH_EMBED_CONTENT_TYPE}']"
    end
end

**Alright, time to synthesize this whole mental walk-through!**

Okay, so I've been digging deep into how this bot integration is working, specifically focusing on handling edge cases and making sure everything is rock solid across all environments. The key here, and what initially grabbed my attention, is the test environment setting: `config.action_dispatch.show_exceptions = :none`. This means any uncaught exceptions (like `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound` or `ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid`) in tests will *raise* an exception, not render a 404 or 422 page. This is fantastic because it forces us to be explicit with our HTTP status codes, and the implications here are HUGE!

My thought process led me to explicitly returning clean HTTP responses (401, 404, 422, 201) in the bot messages controller. This approach ensures consistent behavior across test, development, and production environments. No more unexpected HTML debug pages in `curl`! I've confirmed that using `head :unauthorized`, `head :not_found`, and `head :unprocessable_content` (the correct symbol for 422 in Rack 3/Rails 8.1) makes everything clean and predictable. We're on the right track here.

Next, I meticulously traced the whole process of bot message creation, from authentication (`authenticate_bot`), room finding (`set_room`), and message creation (`@room.messages.create_with_attachment!`) to the broadcasting process. I've dissected all the callbacks and side effects, step-by-step. I've verified:

*   The message's creator is correctly set to `@bot`.
*   A unique `client_message_id` is generated.
*   `Room#receive` logic, correctly marking messages as unread and queuing push notifications. This includes ensuring proper push notifications fire exactly as a human-authored message would.
*   The indexing of the message body in the search index (`Message::Searchable`).
*   The Turbo Stream `append` and `broadcast_unread_room` broadcasts.
*   The rendering of message content, avatar, and author details in the views, making sure everything renders correctly.

I checked all message actions (boost, reply, copy link, edit/delete) and verified the `Current.user.can_administer?(@message)` logic works correctly with the bot's `creator` field. This confirms that admins can manage bot messages.

I then did a really thorough sweep across the entire codebase to make sure there are no other weird interactions. This includes how bots interact with the `User` model, specifically the `role`, `status`, `password_digest`, `email_address`, and `avatar` attributes. The crucial step here is making sure that a bot cannot log in (as they don't have passwords). I've confirmed the use of `has_secure_password validations: false` and how `SessionsController#create` and `Sessions::TransfersController` securely handle user authentication. I'm migrating `password_digest` to be nullable for bots and added a `bot_token` field and a `creator_id`. This lets us track who made the bot.

I also double-checked the `User::Role` enum. I am designing a `User::Bot` concern in the Campfire style.

I then went through the `User::Bot` concern. I am confirming every line works.
The key here is generating the `bot_token` only when a user is a bot, using `has_secure_token :bot_token` with `before_create { self.bot_token ||= generate_bot_token }, if: :bot?`. This keeps the database cleaner (no `bot_token` for human users) and allows for a mechanism to securely wipe the bot's credentials on deactivation. I have considered security with the `bot_token` format.

And, of course, a critical part of this is what happens when a bot is deactivated or deleted. I carefully checked the `User#deactivate` method and its implications on the bots' relationships. The essential point is ensuring a deactivated bot can no longer interact with any room (open, closed, or direct). The crucial step is the `memberships.without_direct_rooms.delete_all` call which stops the bot from being able to post messages.

Let's start by scrutinizing `User::Bot` (`app/models/user/bot.rb`). I see the `belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", optional: true` association, which is as expected. Also, the `has_many :bots, -> { bot }, class_name: "User", foreign_key: :creator_id` association is right. The `before_create :ensure_bot_token, if: :bot?` callback and the `validates :name, presence: true, if: :bot?` validation seem solid, too. The scope `without_bots, -> { not_bot }` looks correct in context.

The helper methods: `new_bot(attributes = {})` correctly uses `bot.new(**attributes, creator: Current.user)` to instantiate the bot, associating it with the current user. Then, `create_bot!(attributes = {})` uses `new_bot(attributes).tap(&:save!)`, which is a neat and common pattern.

Now, let's examine the `authenticate_bot(bot_key)` method. The code to handle the split of `bot_id` and `bot_token`, and the subsequent database query, plus the secure comparison of the bot token against the stored token, looks good.

Next, I'm checking `ensure_bot_token` and the `generate_unique_bot_token` methods. I note the explicit use of `SecureRandom.base58(24)` and the `User.exists?(bot_token: token)` check for uniqueness. It's a solid, straightforward implementation. I remember that `ActiveRecord::SecureToken` offers a built-in `generate_unique_secure_token(length: 24)`, but this approach is perfectly clear. I would argue this implementation is superior due to its explicitness and lack of 'magic'.

Finally, I need to revisit `User#deactivate` in `app/models/user.rb`. The transaction block looks appropriately scoped. It appears to be handling remote connection closing, membership cleanup, and updates to the `status` and `bot_token` fields. The assignment of `nil` to `bot_token` upon deactivation is especially important.

cat <<'EOF' > app/models/user/bot.rb
module User::Bot
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", optional: true
    has_many :bots, -> { bot }, class_name: "User", foreign_key: :creator_id

    before_create :ensure_bot_token, if: :bot?

    validates :name, presence: true, if: :bot?

    scope :without_bots, -> { not_bot }
  end

  class_methods do
    def new_bot(attributes = {})
      bot.new(**attributes.to_h.symbolize_keys, creator: Current.user)
    end

    def create_bot!(attributes = {})
      new_bot(attributes).tap(&:save!)
    end

    def authenticate_bot(bot_key)
      bot_id, bot_token = bot_key.to_s.split("-", 2)
      return nil if bot_id.blank? || bot_token.blank?

      if user = active.bot.find_by(id: bot_id)
        user if user.bot_token.present? && ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare(user.bot_token, bot_token)
      end
    end
  end

  def bot_key
    "#{id}-#{bot_token}" if bot? && bot_token.present?
  end

  private
    def ensure_bot_token
      self.bot_token ||= generate_unique_bot_token
    end

    def generate_unique_bot_token
      loop do
        token = SecureRandom.base58(24)
        break token unless User.exists?(bot_token: token)
      end
    end
end

class SessionsController < ApplicationController
  allow_unauthenticated_access only: %i[ new create ]
  rate_limit to: 10, within: 3.minutes, only: :create, with: -> { render_rejection :too_many_requests }

  before_action :ensure_user_exists, only: :new

  end

    if user = User.active.without_bots.authenticate_by(email_address: params[:email_address], password: params[:password])
      start_new_session_for user
      redirect_to post_authenticating_url
    else
      render_rejection :unauthorized
    end
  end

  def destroy
    remove_push_subscription
    terminate_current_session
    redirect_to root_url
  end

  private
    def ensure_user_exists
      redirect_to first_run_url if User.without_bots.none?
    end

    def render_rejection(status)
      flash.now[:alert] = "Too many requests or unauthorized."
      render :new, status: status
    end

    def remove_push_subscription
      if endpoint = params[:push_subscription_endpoint]
        Push::Subscription.destroy_by(endpoint: endpoint, user_id: Current.user.id)
      end
    end
end

messages.thinking:
**Eureka! Big Breakthroughs from the Test Runner!**

Okay, so I just saw something HUGE in the test runner output, and it's all starting to click. I was staring at this: `Payload: "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅" -> Status: 404`! A 404 inside a `User.transaction do ... end` block? That's just wrong!

The lightbulb finally went off: `grant_membership_to_open_rooms` is an `after_create_commit` callback! That means, within the scope of an *outer* `User.transaction` block – before that outer transaction commits – the `after_create_commit` callbacks *haven't* fired yet. It's like they're waiting in the wings!

Let me step back and think about `grant_membership_to_open_rooms` on the `User` model. Right, it's defined as an `after_create_commit` in `app/models/user.rb`. Now I see why the `UserTest` passes. In Minitest, Rails treats the test wrapper transaction as a "depth 0" transaction. So, when `User.create!` happens directly in the test, the `after_create_commit` fires immediately because the test wrapper behaves in this way: `run_commit_callbacks_on_first_saved_instances_in_transaction`. But in our `rails runner` manual transaction, it *waits* until the *outer* `User.transaction` actually commits.

And there's a second thing I'm seeing! When the payload was `"_method=delete"`, `Rack::MethodOverride` was rewriting `POST` to `DELETE`, which results in a routing error. If I add a small middleware, or a `Content-Type` normalizer before `Rack::MethodOverride` when the `PATH_INFO` matches the regular expression for the messages path, and the `CONTENT_TYPE` starts with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `"_method=delete"` will work directly without the method override even getting in the way.

Time to test this out. I'm going to run a quick test in `bin/rails runner` *without* that outer `User.transaction` wrapper. I'll clean up afterwards in `ensure`, of course. Let's verify that we get the expected `201 Created`, the correct `Location` header to the new message, and the right "Saved" body.

class User::BotTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  setup do
    Current.user = users(:kevin)
  end

  teardown do

  end

  test "create_bot! creates an active bot owned by Current.user with a unique bot_key" do

    assert bot.active?
    assert_equal users(:kevin), bot.creator
    assert bot.bot_token.present?
    assert_equal "#{bot.id}-#{bot.bot_token}", bot.bot_key
    assert_includes users(:kevin).bots, bot
  end

  test "human users do not get a bot_token or bot_key" do
    user = User.create!(name: "Human", email_address: "human@example.com", password: "secret123456")

    assert user.member?
    assert_nil user.bot_token
    assert_nil user.bot_key
    assert_includes User.without_bots, user
  end

  test "bot requires a name" do
    bot = User.new_bot(name: "")
    assert_not bot.valid?
    assert_includes bot.errors[:name], "can't be blank"
  end

  test "new bot automatically joins all open rooms" do
    bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Deploy Bot")

    assert_equal Rooms::Open.pluck(:id).sort, bot.rooms.pluck(:id).sort
    assert_not_includes bot.rooms, rooms(:designers)
  end

  test "new open room grants access to existing active bots but not deactivated bots" do
    active_bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Active Bot")
    deleted_bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Deleted Bot")
    deleted_bot.deactivate

    open_room = Rooms::Open.create!(name: "Announcements", creator: users(:david))

    assert_includes open_room.users, active_bot
    assert_not_includes open_room.users, deleted_bot
  end

  test "authenticate_bot verifies bot_key securely" do
    bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Deploy Bot")

    assert_equal bot, User.authenticate_bot(bot.bot_key)
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("#{bot.id}-wrongtoken")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("999999-#{bot.bot_token}")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("#{users(:david).id}-#{bot.bot_token}")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("malformed_without_dash")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot("")
    assert_nil User.authenticate_bot(nil)
  end

  test "deactivating a bot revokes its bot_key and removes non-direct memberships" do
    bot = User.create_bot!(name: "Deploy Bot")
    old_key = bot.bot_key

    bot.deactivate

    assert_nil bot.bot_token
    assert_nil bot.bot_key

    assert users(:david).can_administer?(bot)
    assert_not users(:jz).can_administer?(bot)
    assert_not bot.can_administer?(bot)
  end
end

      WebPush.expects(:payload_send).times(expected_deliveries).with do |kwargs|
        payload = JSON.parse(kwargs[:message])
        payload["title"] == @room.name &&
          payload.dig("options", "body") == "Deploy Bot: Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅"
      end

      post "/rooms/#{@room.id}/#{@bot.bot_key}/messages",
        params: "Deploy of v1.2.3 finished ✅",
        headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" }
    end

    wait_for_web_push_delivery_pool_tasks(expected_deliveries)
  end

  test "returns 422 Unprocessable Content for empty or whitespace-only body without attachment" do
    assert_no_difference -> { Message.count } do
      post "/rooms/#{@room.id}/#{@bot.bot_key}/messages",
        params: "",
        headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" }
      assert_response :unprocessable_content

      post "/rooms/#{@room.id}/#{@bot.bot_key}/messages",
        params: "   \n\t  ",
        headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => "text/plain" }
      assert_response :unprocessable_content
    end
  end

  test "returns 404 Not Found for nonexistent room id or closed room bot is not a member of" do
    assert_no_difference -> { Message.count } do
      post "/rooms/99999999/#{@bot.bot_key}/messages", params: "Hello"
      assert_response :not_found

      post "/rooms/bad-room/#{@bot.bot_key}/messages", params: "Hello"
      assert_response :not_found

      # Closed room that @bot has not joined
      assert_not_includes @bot.rooms, rooms(:designers)
      post "/rooms/#{rooms(:designers).id}/#{@bot.bot_key}/messages", params: "Hello"
      assert_response :not_found
    end

    # Once added to the closed room, bot can post
    rooms(:designers).memberships.grant_to(@bot)
    post "/rooms/#{rooms(:designers).id}/#{@bot.bot_key}/messages", params: "Hello Designers"
    assert_response :created
  end

  test "returns 401 Unauthorized for invalid bot code" do
    assert_no_difference -> { Message.count } do
      post "/rooms/#{@room.id}/invalid-bot-code/messages", params: "Hello"
      assert_response :unauthorized

      post "/rooms/#{@room.id}/#{@bot.id}-wrongtoken/messages", params: "Hello"
      assert_response :unauthorized

      post "/rooms/#{@room.id}/bad.code.with.dots/messages", params: "Hello"
      assert_response :unauthorized

      # Invalid bot code with bad room id still returns 401 Unauthorized without leaking room existence
      post "/rooms/99999999/invalid-bot-code/messages", params: "Hello"
      assert_response :unauthorized
    end
  end

  test "deleted bot can no longer post messages while keeping previous messages" do
    post "/rooms/#{@room.id}/#{@bot.bot_key}/messages", params: "Before deletion"
    assert_response :created
    previous_message = Message.last

    old_key = @bot.bot_key
    @bot.deactivate

    assert_no_difference -> { Message.count } do
      post "/rooms/#{@room.id}/#{old_key}/messages", params: "After deletion"
      assert_response :unauthorized
    end

    assert previous_message.reload.persisted?
    assert_equal "Deploy Bot", previous_message.creator.name
  end

  private
    def wait_for_web_push_delivery_pool_tasks(count)
      pool = Rails.configuration.x.web_push_pool.delivery_pool
      start = Time.now
      while pool.completed_task_count < count
        raise "Timeout waiting for web push pool tasks" if Time.now - start > 1.0
        sleep 0.02
      end
    end
end

require "socket"

require "json"

require "uri"

class SimpleCDP
  def initialize(ws_url)
    uri = URI(ws_url)
    @sock = TCPSocket.new(uri.host, uri.port)
    key = Base64.strict_encode64("1234567890123456")
    handshake = "GET #{uri.request_uri} HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: #{uri.host}:#{uri.port}\r\nUpgrade: websocket\r\nConnection: Upgrade\r\nSec-WebSocket-Key: #{key}\r\nSec-WebSocket-Version: 13\r\n\r\n"
    @sock.write(handshake)
    header = +""
    header << @sock.gets until header.end_with?("\r\n\r\n")
    raise "WS handshake failed: #{header}" unless header.include?("101")
    @id = 0
    @events = []
  end

  def call(method, params = {})
    @id += 1
    target_id = @id
    send_frame(JSON.generate({ id: target_id, method: method, params: params }))
    loop do
      msg = JSON.parse(read_frame)
      if msg["id"] == target_id
        raise "CDP error: #{msg['error']}" if msg["error"]
        return msg["result"]
      else
        @events << msg
      end
    end
  end

  def drain_events(timeout = 0.2)
    while IO.select([@sock], nil, nil, timeout)
      msg = JSON.parse(read_frame)
      @events << msg
    end
    @events
  end

  def eval_js(expr)
    res = call("Runtime.evaluate", { expression: expr, returnByValue: true, awaitPromise: true })
    raise "JS exception: #{res['exceptionDetails']}" if res["exceptionDetails"]
    res.dig("result", "value")
  end

  def wait_for(desc, timeout: 8)
    deadline = Time.now + timeout
    loop do
      drain_events(0.05)
      val = yield
      return val if val
      raise "Timeout waiting for: #{desc}" if Time.now > deadline
      sleep 0.1
    end
  end

  private
    def send_frame(str)
      bytes = str.b
      len = bytes.bytesize
      header = [0x81].pack("C")
      if len < 126
        header << [0x80 | len].pack("C")
      elsif len < 65536
        header << [0x80 | 126, len].pack("Cn")
      else
        header << [0x80 | 127, len].pack("CQ>")
      end
      mask = [1, 2, 3, 4]
      header << mask.pack("C4")
      masked = bytes.bytes.each_with_index.map { |b, i| b ^ mask[i % 4] }.pack("C*")
      @sock.write(header + masked)
    end

    def read_frame
      b1, b2 = @sock.read(2).unpack("CC")
      len = b2 & 0x7f
      if len == 126
        len = @sock.read(2).unpack1("n")
      elsif len == 127
        len = @sock.read(8).unpack1("Q>")
      end
      mask = (b2 & 0x80) != 0 ? @sock.read(4).bytes : nil
      payload = @sock.read(len)
      if mask
        payload = payload.bytes.each_with_index.map { |b, i| b ^ mask[i % 4] }.pack("C*")
      end
      payload.force_encoding("UTF-8")
    end
end

require "socket"
require "net/http"
require "json"
require "fileutils"
require "base64"
require "uri"

class SimpleCDP
  def initialize(ws_url)
    uri = URI(ws_url)
    @sock = TCPSocket.new(uri.host, uri.port)
    key = Base64.strict_encode64("1234567890123456")
    handshake = "GET #{uri.request_uri} HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: #{uri.host}:#{uri.port}\r\nUpgrade: websocket\r\nConnection: Upgrade\r\nSec-WebSocket-Key: #{key}\r\nSec-WebSocket-Version: 13\r\n\r\n"
    @sock.write(handshake)
    header = +""
    header << @sock.gets until header.end_with?("\r\n\r\n")
    raise "WS handshake failed: #{header}" unless header.include?("101")
    @id = 0
    @events = []
  end

  def call(method, params = {})
    @id += 1
    target_id = @id
    send_frame(JSON.generate({ id: target_id, method: method, params: params }))
    loop do
      msg = JSON.parse(read_frame)
      if msg["id"] == target_id
        raise "CDP error: #{msg['error']}" if msg["error"]
        return msg["result"]
      else
        @events << msg
      end
    end
  end

  def drain_events(timeout = 0.2)
    while IO.select([@sock], nil, nil, timeout)
      msg = JSON.parse(read_frame)
      @events << msg
    end
    @events
  end

  def eval_js(expr)
    res = call("Runtime.evaluate", { expression: expr, returnByValue: true, awaitPromise: true })
    raise "JS exception: #{res['exceptionDetails']}" if res["exceptionDetails"]
    res.dig("result", "value")
  end

  def wait_for(desc, timeout: 8)
    deadline = Time.now + timeout
    loop do
      drain_events(0.05)
      val = yield
      return val if val
      raise "Timeout waiting for: #{desc}" if Time.now > deadline
      sleep 0.1
    end
  end

  private
    def send_frame(str)
      bytes = str.b
      len = bytes.bytesize
      header = [0x81].pack("C")
      if len < 126
        header << [0x80 | len].pack("C")
      elsif len < 65536
        header << [0x80 | 126, len].pack("Cn")
      else
        header << [0x80 | 127, len].pack("CQ>")
      end
      mask = [1, 2, 3, 4]
      header << mask.pack("C4")
      masked = bytes.bytes.each_with_index.map { |b, i| b ^ mask[i % 4] }.pack("C*")
      @sock.write(header + masked)
    end

    def read_frame
      b1, b2 = @sock.read(2).unpack("CC")
      len = b2 & 0x7f
      if len == 126
        len = @sock.read(2).unpack1("n")
      elsif len == 127
        len = @sock.read(8).unpack1("Q>")
      end
      mask = (b2 & 0x80) != 0 ? @sock.read(4).bytes : nil
      payload = @sock.read(len)
      if mask
        payload = payload.bytes.each_with_index.map { |b, i| b ^ mask[i % 4] }.pack("C*")
      end
      payload.force_encoding("UTF-8")
    end
end

      post_bot_message rooms(:designers).id, @bot.bot_key, "Hello"
      assert_response :not_found
    end

    # Once added to the closed room, bot can post
    rooms(:designers).memberships.grant_to(@bot)
    post_bot_message rooms(:designers).id, @bot.bot_key, "Hello Designers"
    assert_response :created
  end

  test "returns 401 Unauthorized for invalid bot code" do
    assert_no_difference -> { Message.count } do
      post_bot_message @room.id, "invalid-bot-code", "Hello"
      assert_response :unauthorized

      post_bot_message @room.id, "#{@bot.id}-wrongtoken", "Hello"
      assert_response :unauthorized

      post_bot_message @room.id, "bad.code.with.dots", "Hello"
      assert_response :unauthorized

      # Invalid bot code with bad room id still returns 401 Unauthorized without leaking room existence
      post_bot_message 99999999, "invalid-bot-code", "Hello"
      assert_response :unauthorized
    end
  end

  test "deleted bot can no longer post messages while keeping previous messages" do
    post_bot_message @room.id, @bot.bot_key, "Before deletion"
    assert_response :created
    previous_message = Message.last

    old_key = @bot.bot_key
    @bot.deactivate

    assert_no_difference -> { Message.count } do
      post_bot_message @room.id, old_key, "After deletion"
      assert_response :unauthorized
    end

    assert previous_message.reload.persisted?
    assert_equal "Deploy Bot", previous_message.creator.name
  end

  private
    def post_bot_message(room_id, bot_key, body, content_type: "application/x-www-form-urlencoded")
      post "/rooms/#{room_id}/#{bot_key}/messages",
        params: +body,
        headers: { "CONTENT_TYPE" => content_type }
    end

    def wait_for_web_push_delivery_pool_tasks(count)
      pool = Rails.configuration.x.web_push_pool.delivery_pool
      start = Time.now
      while pool.completed_task_count < count
        raise "Timeout waiting for web push pool tasks" if Time.now - start > 1.0
        sleep 0.02
      end
    end
end

cat <<'EOF' > docs/bots.md
# Chat Bots Design Notes

## Data Model (`User` + `User::Bot`)

Bots are represented in the `users` table with `role: :bot` (`enum :role, %i[ member administrator bot ]`):

- **`creator_id`**: Foreign key to `users` (`belongs_to :creator, class_name: "User", optional: true`), recording which chat member created the bot. Because `User::Role#can_administer?` checks `administrator? || self == record&.creator`, creators and administrators automatically have permission to manage a bot while other regular members do not.
- **`bot_token` & `bot_key`**: Active bots receive a unique 24-character `SecureRandom.base58` `bot_token` on creation. The externally visible bot code (`User#bot_key`) is `"#{id}-#{bot_token}"`. `User.authenticate_bot(bot_key)` looks up the active bot by primary key `id` and compares `bot_token` in constant time via `ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare`.
- **Deactivation (Deletion)**: Deleting a bot calls `User#deactivate`, which sets `status: :deactivated`, clears `bot_token: nil`, and removes non-direct room memberships while preserving historical messages authored by the bot.
- **Room Memberships**: Because bots are `User` records with `status: :active`, they automatically join all open rooms via `after_create_commit :grant_membership_to_open_rooms` (and `Rooms::Open#grant_access_to_all_users`) and appear alongside human users in closed/direct room member selectors (`User.active`). Human-only flows (`/account/edit` member list, `/session`, session transfers, IP bans) scope queries with `User.without_bots`.

## Bot HTTP API (`Messages::ByBotsController`)

- **Endpoint**: `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_key/messages` (`constraints: { room_id: /[^\/]+/, bot_key: /[^\/]+/ }`).
- **Raw Body Handling**: `curl -d "..."` sends `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` by default even though the payload is raw text (which may contain `%`, `+`, `&`, etc.). `Messages::ByBotsController` sets `wrap_parameters false` and `request.request_parameters = {}` in `process_action` before Rails instrumentation accesses `request.filtered_parameters`, preventing Rack/Rails form/JSON parameter parsers from raising `400 Bad Request` on raw bodies. The raw UTF-8 body is read from `request.raw_post`.
- **Validation & Extension Point for Attachments**: `Message` validates `ensure_body_or_attachment_present` (`body.blank? && body.body&.attachables.blank? && !attachment?`). If future features add file attachment uploads for bots (e.g., binary bodies by `Content-Type` or `multipart/form-data`), `Messages::ByBotsController#create` can attach the file and call `@message.process_attachment` before `@message.broadcast_create`.
- **Broadcasts & Push Notifications**: Setting `Current.user = bot` sets `message.creator = bot`. Saving triggers `Room#receive` (`unread_memberships` + `Room::PushMessageJob`), and `@message.broadcast_create` appends the message via Turbo Streams and notifies `UnreadRoomsChannel`.
EOF

I have implemented chat bots in Campfire along with UI management and the HTTP message posting API:

- **Model & Schema (`User::Bot`, `User::Role`, `Message`)**:
  - Extended `User` roles with `:bot` (`enum :role, %i[ member administrator bot ]`), nullable `password_digest`, `creator_id` reference, and unique `bot_token` (`bot_key` formatted as `<id>-<bot_token>` verified in constant time via `ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare` and filtered in Rails logs).
  - New bots automatically join all open rooms and can be added to closed and direct rooms the same way as people (`User.active`), while human-only flows (`/account/edit` member list, sessions, session transfers, IP bans) scope queries with `User.without_bots`.
  - Deleting a bot deactivates it (`status: :deactivated`), clears its `bot_token` so it can no longer post messages, and preserves previously posted messages.
  - Added `Message` validation requiring a non-blank body or attachment.

- **Bot Management UI (`BotsController`, `app/views/bots/`, `app/views/accounts/edit.html.erb`)**:
  - Added the `"Set up chat bots"` bot icon link on `/account/edit` for all chat members.
  - Created `/bots` listing the current user's bots (or all bots for administrators) on a single page without pagination, with the `"Add a chat bot"` button, each bot's name, read-only `"Bot code"` input, and `"Edit <bot name>"` link in the same list item.
  - Created `/bots/new` and `/bots/:id/edit` sharing the form with optional avatar upload, required `"Name the bot"` field, `"Save changes"` button, and on edit the `"Delete this chat bot"` button using native browser confirmation (`data-turbo-confirm`).

- **HTTP Bot Message API (`Messages::ByBotsController`)**:
  - Added `POST /rooms/:room_id/:bot_key/messages` accepting raw request bodies directly (`201 Created` with `Location: /messages/:message_id`, `422 Unprocessable Content` for empty body without attachment, `404 Not Found` for invalid/inaccessible room ID, `401 Unauthorized` for invalid or deleted bot code), broadcasting via Turbo Streams / `UnreadRoomsChannel` and triggering Web Push notifications identically to human-authored messages.

- **Documentation & Tests**:
  - Added design notes in `docs/bots.md` and model/controller/integration tests in `test/models/user/bot_test.rb`, `test/controllers/bots_controller_test.rb`, and `test/controllers/messages/by_bots_controller_test.rb`.
